findings.effect: English loanwords with accents count as Spanish orthography. Two lowercase accented loanwords and fewer than two English stopwords are enough to classify a reply as Spanish.
findings.reason: An English reply such as “Saved café résumé.” contributes two distinct accented words and zero English stopwords, so detectReplyLanguage incorrectly classifies it as Spanish.

findings.effect: Spanish content words count even when capitalized because the text is lowercased and the content-word check has no proper-noun guard. English replies containing Spanish names or addresses can therefore be classified as Spanish and fail when English is expected.
findings.reason: Capitalized names are lowercased before content-word matching, so an English reply such as “Saved El Perfil.” gains enough Spanish evidence to fail the English language check.

findings.effect: Capitalized proper nouns count as Spanish content words because the text is lowercased before content-word matching, without a capitalization guard. One Spanish stopword plus one capitalized content word reaches the threshold, causing English replies containing Spanish names or addresses to fail.
findings.reason: The new content-word evidence makes “Saved El Perfil.” reach the Spanish threshold through the stopword “el” and capitalized name “Perfil,” incorrectly failing an English reply.
